package_info.why_malicious: Versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 of xz-utils contain a supply chain backdoor (CVE-2024-3094) introduced via a malicious M4 macro in the tarball source distribution. This macro injects unauthorized code during the build process, resulting in compromised liblzma binaries that enable remote, unauthenticated attackers to interfere with SSHD authentication and potentially gain unauthorized system access.

execution_context.file_location: m4 macro file in tarball source distribution (e.g., m4/build-to-host.m4 or similar)
required_permissions: filesystem (write access to build output directories)
build environment (ability to execute build scripts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: A malicious, obfuscated M4 macro is embedded in the tarball source distribution. During the build process, this macro conditionally compiles and injects unauthorized code into the xz-utils binaries, specifically targeting the liblzma library. The macro is not present in the official Git repository and is designed to evade detection by standard code review.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build-time, the malicious M4 macro executes, conditionally compiling and injecting unauthorized code into the liblzma library, resulting in a compromised binary that contains a hidden backdoor.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of an undocumented, obfuscated M4 macro in the tarball source that alters the build output is highly suspicious, especially since it is absent from the official Git repository. Such macros are not expected to introduce hidden functionality or modify authentication mechanisms.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard build macros are used for configuration and portability, not for injecting hidden code or altering security-critical components. Here, the macro surreptitiously introduces a backdoor into the build output without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: M4 macros are legitimately used to configure build parameters or enable/disable features, but never to inject hidden authentication bypasses or unauthorized code into binaries.
key_indicators: Obfuscated or undocumented M4 macro present only in tarball source distribution
Macro triggers compilation of code not present in mainline source or official Git repository
Build artifacts differ from those produced from official source

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when SSHD loads the compromised liblzma library)
execution_context.file_location: compiled xz-utils library (liblzma.so) on the target system
required_permissions: process memory (ability to execute within SSHD process context)
potentially network (if exfiltration or remote command/control is attempted)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The injected code within the compromised liblzma library hooks into SSHD authentication routines at runtime. When SSHD loads the tainted liblzma, the malicious code intercepts authentication logic, enabling remote, unauthenticated attackers to bypass normal authentication and gain unauthorized access.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when SSHD loads the compromised liblzma library, the injected code hooks into SSHD authentication routines, intercepts authentication data flow, and enables remote, unauthenticated access by bypassing standard authentication checks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Compression libraries like liblzma should not interact with or alter authentication mechanisms of unrelated services such as SSHD. The code is specifically designed to subvert SSHD authentication, which is a critical security violation and a clear indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate compression libraries are not expected to interact with authentication logic or provide any mechanism for remote access. The presence of authentication hooks in liblzma is a severe deviation from expected behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases where a compression library would hook into or modify SSHD authentication routines.
key_indicators: liblzma library contains code that hooks or intercepts SSHD authentication routines
Enables remote, unauthenticated access to the system via SSHD
Malicious behavior only present in binaries built from the compromised tarball, not from official Git sources
Altered control flow or unexpected code paths in liblzma.so

attack_chain.action: A malicious, obfuscated M4 macro in the tarball source distribution triggers the injection of unauthorized backdoor code into the liblzma library during the build process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Compromised xz-utils binaries, specifically liblzma.so, are produced with hidden backdoor functionality.

attack_chain.action: The compromised xz-utils library (liblzma.so) is installed on the target system and subsequently loaded by SSHD during normal operation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Runtime execution of the injected backdoor code within the SSHD process context.

attack_chain.action: The injected code in liblzma.so intercepts SSHD authentication routines at runtime, enabling remote, unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized system access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves unauthorized access to the target system via SSHD.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of undocumented or obfuscated M4 macros in build scripts of xz-utils tarball source
xz-utils binaries (liblzma.so) exhibiting unexpected code paths or authentication hooks not present in official builds
liblzma library interfering with or hooking into SSHD authentication routines at runtime
file_indicators: M4 macro files in tarball source distribution (e.g., m4/build-to-host.m4) not present in the official Git repository
xz-utils binaries (liblzma.so) with cryptographic hashes differing from those of official, known-good builds
liblzma.so containing additional or obfuscated code sections not present in official releases
network_indicators: Unusual SSHD authentication attempts succeeding without valid credentials (e.g., logins without correct passwords or keys)
Potential outbound network connections initiated by SSHD or liblzma.so if exfiltration or command/control is attempted (not confirmed in this report)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Compare xz-utils tarball source and build artifacts against the official Git repository and known-good binaries. Inspect build scripts for undocumented or obfuscated M4 macros. Use file integrity monitoring to detect altered liblzma.so binaries by comparing cryptographic hashes. Analyze liblzma.so for unexpected code paths or authentication hooks. Monitor SSHD logs for unexpected authentication successes or anomalies. Employ runtime analysis to detect unauthorized interactions between liblzma.so and SSHD authentication routines.
